Troubleshooting

Source: vignettes/troubleshooting.Rmd
troubleshooting.Rmd
library(agetime)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

This vignette describes errors and difficulties you might encounter when using agetime, and suggests solutions.

Reading labels

“Don’t know how to interpret label”

Problem

A label is in a format that agetime does not recognize.

x <- c("0-4", "5-9", "Everything", "85+ (a)")
age_standard(x)
#> Error in `age_standard()`:
#> ! Don't know how to interpret 2 labels: "Everything" and "85+ (a)".

Solution

The error message lists the labels that cannot be interpreted. Clean these labels before passing them to agetime.

x_clean <- x
x_clean[x_clean == "Everything"] <- "Total"
x_clean[x_clean == "85+ (a)"] <- "85+"
age_standard(x_clean)
#> [1] "0-4"   "5-9"   "Total" "85+"

Discussion

agetime recognizes many common formats, including:

  • ranges such as "5-9", "5 to 9", "5--9", and "5-9 years";
  • open age groups such as "85+", "85 and over", "85 or more", "85 years and older", and "85 & over";
  • age groups starting at 0, such as "Under 5", "less than 5", "<5", and "Infant";
  • ages from 0 up to and including a stated age, such as "5 or younger" and "5 and younger", which become "0-5";
  • totals such as "Total" and "All ages", and
  • missing values such as "Not stated", "Unknown", and "Age not stated".

Case, spaces, and leading zeros are ignored.

One-year periods written as ranges

Problem

A period label such as "2020-2021" gives an error.

period_standard("2020-2021")
#> Error in `period_standard()`:
#> ! Label "2020-2021" describes a one-year period.
#> ℹ With `interpret_multi` = "at_upper", "2020-2021" is the interval [2020,
#>   2021).
#> ℹ Write one-year periods as a single year, e.g. "2020"?
#> ℹ Or set `interpret_multi` to "below_upper" if "2020-2021" is meant to be two
#>   years?

Solution

By default, period and cohort functions read "2020-2021" as the interval from the start of 2020 to the start of 2021, which is a single year. agetime expects single years to be written as "2020". If "2020-2021" denotes the two-year period consisting of the years 2020 and 2021, then set interpret_multi to "below_upper".

period_standard("2020-2021", interpret_multi = "below_upper")
#> [1] "2020-2022"

See Also

  • The section on rules for interpreting inputs in ?period_lower

Financial and academic years: “Lower limit greater than upper limit”

Problem

Financial and academic years that start part way through the calendar year are sometimes described using labels such as "2019/20" or "2019-20". agetime currently does not know how to interpret these labels. For instance, it interprets "2019/20" as describing a period that starts in the year 2019 and ends in the year 20.

period_standard("2019/20")
#> Error in `period_standard()`:
#> ! Label "2019/20" invalid.
#> ℹ Lower limit greater than upper limit.
#> ℹ With `interpret_multi` = "at_upper", "2019/20" is the interval [2019, 20).

Solution

Calculate the end year and pass it to agetime with interpret_single set to "upper".

fy <- c("2019/20", "2020-21", "1999/00")
fy_end <- as.integer(substr(fy, 1L, 4L)) + 1
fy_end
#> [1] 2020 2021 2000
period_interval(fy_end, interpret_single = "upper")
#> [1] "[2019, 2020)" "[2020, 2021)" "[1999, 2000)"
period_mid(fy_end, interpret_single = "upper")
#> [1] 2019.5 2020.5 1999.5

The same approach works for cohorts.

See Also

  • The section on rules for interpreting inputs in ?period_lower and ?cohort_lower

Single-year periods that appear to overlap with open intervals

Problem

When the labels for single-year periods are based on the upper limits of the periods, the labels can appear to overlap with open intervals. In the series "2019", "2020", "2020+", for instance, the label "2020" appears to overlap with the label "2020+".

Solution

Although they look strange, series such as "2019", "2020", "2020+" are in fact valid, if they use the upper-limit convention. To see what is going on, use period_interval().

period_interval(c("2019", "2020", "2020+"), interpret_single = "upper")
#> [1] "[2018, 2019)" "[2019, 2020)" "[2020, Inf)"

The "2020" label might refer, for instance, to the period that starts at midnight on 1 July 2019 and ends at midnight on 1 July 2020, while the "2020+" label refers to the period that starts at midnight on 1 July 2020.

Discussion

Series that use the upper-limit labelling convention and that have open periods or cohorts are rare.

See Also

  • Financial and academic years
  • period_interval() and cohort_interval()
  • The section on rules for interpreting inputs in ?period_lower and ?cohort_lower

Checking labels

Different labels for the same age group

Problem

age_assert_values() or age_diagnose_values() reports an overlap, even though the age groups look distinct.

x <- c("0", "infant", "1-4", "5+")
age_assert_values(x, no_overlap = TRUE)
#> Error in `age_assert_values()`:
#> ! Age group labels fail check `no_overlap`.
#> ✖ `no_overlap`: Example of overlap among values: '0' and 'infant' describe the
#>   same interval.

Solution

Two different labels, "0" and "infant", describe the same age group. Standardizing the labels makes this visible.

age_standard(x)
#> [1] "0"   "0"   "1-4" "5+"

You will then need to decide what to do about the repeated values. See Overlaps in a data frame with repeated age groups for one possible approach.

Overlaps in a data frame with repeated age groups

Problem

age_assert_values() reports an overlap in a column of a data frame where each age group appears once for each sex, region, or year.

df <- tibble(
  age = c("0-4", "5-9", "0-4", "5-9"),
  sex = c("F", "F", "M", "M")
)
df |>
  mutate(age = age_assert_values(age, no_overlap = TRUE))
#> Error in `mutate()`:
#> ℹ In argument: `age = age_assert_values(age, no_overlap = TRUE)`.
#> Caused by error in `age_assert_values()`:
#> ! Age group labels fail check `no_overlap`.
#> ✖ `no_overlap`: Example of overlap among values: '0-4' appears 2 times. To
#>   allow repeats, such as one per sex, check within groups, for instance using
#>   dplyr::group_by().

Solution

Check within groups.

df |>
  group_by(sex) |>
  mutate(age = age_assert_values(age, no_overlap = TRUE))
#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
#> # Groups:   sex [2]
#>   age   sex  
#>   <chr> <chr>
#> 1 0-4   F    
#> 2 5-9   F    
#> 3 0-4   M    
#> 4 5-9   M

See Also

  • Cookbook: Check labels within groups of a data frame

Totals and missing values

Problem

A check fails, or a function such as age_extend() or age_coarsen_to() gives an error, because the labels include a total or a missing value.

x <- c("0-4", "5-9", "Total")
age_assert_values(x, no_total = TRUE)
#> Error in `age_assert_values()`:
#> ! Age group labels fail check `no_total`.
#> ✖ `no_total`: Example among values: 'Total'.

Solution

Use age_is_total() and age_is_missing() to find the labels for totals or missing values. If appropriate, remove the associated rows.

df <- tibble(
  age = c("0-4", "5-9", "Total", "Not stated"),
  count = c(10, 20, 35, 5)
)

df |>
  filter(!age_is_total(age), !age_is_missing(age))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#>   age   count
#>   <chr> <dbl>
#> 1 0-4      10
#> 2 5-9      20

Discussion

age_coarsen(), age_coarsen_five(), and similar functions keep totals and missing values as separate categories, so they do not need to be removed first.

See Also

  • Cookbook: Drop totals from a dataset and Drop “Not stated” categories from a dataset

Transforming labels

Coarsening fails

Problem

age_coarsen(), age_coarsen_to(), or one of their variants gives an error.

x <- c("0-4", "5-9", "12")
age_coarsen(x, breaks = c(0, 7, 10))
#> Error in `age_coarsen()`:
#> ! Can't coarsen age groups.
#> ✖ Age group "5-9" would be split by the new age groups.
#> ℹ "5-9" overlaps "0-6" and "7-9".
#> ✖ Age group "12" is not fully covered by the new age groups.
#> ℹ New age groups cover [0, 10).
#> ℹ Set `open_right = TRUE` to include age groups above 10?

Solution

The error message distinguishes two problems:

  • A label would be split when it overlaps two or more new age groups. In the case above, "5-9" overlaps "0-6" and "7-9". When a label would be split, move the breaks so that they fall between the old age groups.
  • A label is not fully covered when it lies partly or wholly outside the new age groups. In the case above, "12" lies above 10. When a label is not fully covered, add breaks, or, for age_coarsen(), set open_right = TRUE.
age_coarsen(x, breaks = c(0, 10), open_right = TRUE)
#> [1] 0-9 0-9 10+
#> Levels: 0-9 10+

With age_coarsen_to(), every label must lie inside one of the labels in to. Add labels to to, or remove labels that should not be included.

Unused levels disappear from tables

Problem

You used a fill function to add age, period, or cohort levels, but tidyverse functions count() or summarise() drop these levels if they have no observations.

df <- tibble(
  age = c("0-4", "10-14", "0-4"),
  respondents = c(10, 20, 5)
) |>
  mutate(age = age_fill(age))

levels(df$age)
#> [1] "0-4"   "5-9"   "10-14"

df |>
  count(age)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#>   age       n
#>   <fct> <int>
#> 1 0-4       2
#> 2 10-14     1

Solution

Tidyverse functions drop unused factor levels by default. Use .drop = FALSE to retain the unused levels.

df |>
  count(age, .drop = FALSE)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   age       n
#>   <fct> <int>
#> 1 0-4       2
#> 2 5-9       0
#> 3 10-14     1

df |>
  group_by(age, .drop = FALSE) |>
  summarise(respondents = sum(respondents))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   age   respondents
#>   <fct>       <dbl>
#> 1 0-4            15
#> 2 5-9             0
#> 3 10-14          20

See Also

  • Cookbook: Include levels that don’t appear in the data

Results are factors, not character vectors

Problem

age_coarsen(), age_fill(), age_set_open_right(), and age_set_order() return factors. They do this because factor levels can contain useful information, such as labels that do not appear in the data. But sometimes the task calls for a character vector, not a factor.

x <- c("0", "1-4", "5-9")
x |>
  age_coarsen_five()
#> [1] 0-4 0-4 5-9
#> Levels: 0-4 5-9

Solution

Call as.character() on the result.

x |>
  age_coarsen_five() |>
  as.character()
#> [1] "0-4" "0-4" "5-9"

Midpoints of open age groups

Problem

age_mid() gives an error for an open age group within a grouped calculation.

df <- tibble(
  sex = c("F", "F", "M"),
  age = c("80-84", "85+", "85+")
)

df |>
  group_by(sex) |>
  mutate(mid = age_mid(age))
#> Error in `mutate()`:
#> ℹ In argument: `mid = age_mid(age)`.
#> ℹ In group 2: `sex = "M"`.
#> Caused by error in `age_mid()`:
#> ! Can't calculate midpoint of open age group "85+".
#> ℹ No closed age groups to take a width from.

Solution

age_mid() gives an open age group a midpoint based on the width of the nearest closed age group. In the group sex = "M", there is no closed age group. Calculate midpoints before grouping.

df |>
  mutate(mid = age_mid(age))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>   sex   age     mid
#>   <chr> <chr> <dbl>
#> 1 F     80-84  82.5
#> 2 F     85+    87.5
#> 3 M     85+    87.5
